newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa mulls health warnings on alcohol packaging.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa mulls health warnings on alcohol packaging.

text.p: South Africa's Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma, spurred by the country's high alcohol consumption, is considering measures to package alcoholic drinks with health warnings, a spokesman said on Thursday.

"It's a question of trying to normalise society's behaviour and also look at innovative ways to ensure that the little budget that we have is utilised to the optimum without being overburdened by preventable instances like road accidents caused by drunken people," Zuma's spokesman Vincent Hlongwane told Reuters.
He said a recent study conducted by the health ministry put South Africa's consumption of alchol, including beer and spirits, at six billion litres a year.

"It (the figure) has been well researched and we view it as excessive. The fact of the matter is that we've got a responsibility for the health of this nation," Hlongwane said, adding that the ministry did not intend stopping people from drinking through such measures.

"Alchohol...has very serious effects in terms of violence, family break-ups, rapes, child and spouse abuse and road accidents here. The number of road accidents we're seeing in this country is alarming.

"No minister of health who is in his or her senses would say people should stop drinking. All we are appealing for and all we are trying to do is that people use alcohol in moderation and they should be aware that if it's...abused...it's got very serious effects," Hlongwane said.
He said there were no immediate plans to table legislation in parliament before all concerned parties had been consulted.
But beverage, hotel and leisure industry analysts said the warnings would put no brake on people's urge to drink.

"I imagine people carrying on drinking alcohol whether there are health warnings or not. I don't think it's going to help. We have health warnings on cigarettes but people are still smoking," one analyst, who did not want to be named, told Reuters.
"I think it is probably a bit extreme to have warnings on alcohol bottles, but I don't think they're going to destroy the industry," he told Reuters.

Asked what the ministry would do if the liquor industry picked a fight with them over the issue, Hlongwane said: "They should actually fight people who are consumers of their alcohol and begin to engage them in an education campaign on how to take alcohol."
